title: What Is Wheelchair (Vintage)? — Definition
body:
Medical technology before the modern era: the monaural stethoscope, ether inhalers, iron lungs, early X-ray apparatus, apothecary balances, leech jars, cupping sets, trephines, and the nursing and surgical tools that carried medicine from craft toward science. Presented as history of technology; not medical advice.

In the context of this database, the Wheelchair (Vintage) is presented as one medical history record among the historical medical devices family. 1655's Farffler: the 1655 — the 1933's folding.

title: Origins and History of Wheelchair (Vintage)
body:
The Wheelchair (Vintage) belongs to the 1600s–1950s era and traces to Various.

Laënnec's wooden stethoscope (1816) let doctors hear the chest; the binaural version (1851) perfected it. Ether anesthesia (1846) and Lister's antisepsis (1867) made surgery survivable; X-rays (1895) made the body visible — early tubes burned operators before safety. The iron lung (1928) breathed for polio patients; the heart-lung machine (1953) enabled open-heart surgery. Apothecaries weighed grains and drams on hand balances; patent-medicine showmen sold hope in bottles. Nursing (Nightingale, Civil War) professionalized care; the thermometer and sphygmomanometer quantified the body.

Within that longer story, Wheelchair (Vintage): The 1655; the 1933 Everest & Jennings. The chair is the mobility's wheels.

title: How Wheelchair (Vintage) Works
body:
Acoustic devices channel body sounds: the stethoscope's chestpiece diaphragm/bell couples vibrations to air columns in the binaurals. Ether inhalers vaporized anesthetic over gauze or in closed masks. Iron lungs sealed the body in a chamber, alternating pressure to move the chest wall. Early X-ray used Crookes tubes with no shielding — fluoroscopy glowed live. Apothecary balances compared unknown powders against grain weights with knife-edge pivots. Cupping and leeching drew blood on humoral theory — now historical practice, not recommendation.

Applied to the Wheelchair (Vintage) (1600s–1950s, Various): The chair is the mobility's wheels.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Wheelchair (Vintage) in Culture
body:
The doctor's black bag — stethoscope, thermometer, tongue depressors — is an icon of trust. Iron lungs in polio wards are a generation's memory; the polio vaccine ended them. Apothecary jars are design classics; the mortar and pestle still marks every pharmacy. Early X-ray's burns taught radiation safety the hard way.

The Wheelchair (Vintage) carries that cultural charge directly: The chair is the mobility's wheels.

title: Wheelchair (Vintage) Restoration Guide
body:
Clean brass and glass gently; replace perished rubber tubing with modern equivalents. X-ray tubes are display-only — never energize. Document provenance; medical artifacts carry ethical weight — collect respectfully.

Restoration order for a Wheelchair (Vintage): 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical medical history record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: Wheelchair (Vintage) — Apothecary unit converter (Runnable Python)
body:
Converts historical apothecary weights (grains, scruples, drams, ounces) to metric — the units every prescription used before grams.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Wheelchair (Vintage) so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Apothecary <-> metric converter (public-domain historical units)
# 20 grains = 1 scruple; 3 scruples = 1 dram; 8 drams = 1 ounce (480 grains)
GRAIN_G = 0.06479891

def apothecary_to_g(oz=0, dr=0, scr=0, gr=0):
    grains = oz*480 + dr*60 + scr*20 + gr
    return grains * GRAIN_G

def g_to_apothecary(g):
    grains = g / GRAIN_G
    oz = int(grains // 480); grains -= oz*480
    dr = int(grains // 60); grains -= dr*60
    scr = int(grains // 20); grains -= scr*20
    return oz, dr, scr, round(grains, 1)

print("2 drams 1 scruple =", round(apothecary_to_g(dr=2, scr=1), 2), "g")
print("5 g =", "%doz %ddr %dscr %.1fgr" % g_to_apothecary(5))
print("1 grain =", GRAIN_G*1000, "mg  (aspirin tablet ~5 grains)")
